query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of titanium into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy to promote the in situ formation of nano‐scale TiC precipitates will simultaneously improve mechanical integrity by toughening grain boundaries and inhibiting crack propagation while preserving the large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The rare‐earth–free (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy as conventionally arc-melted and homogenized, which exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but with poor fracture integrity.
generation.intervention: Add a minor titanium content (on the order of 1–3 atomic percent) to the base alloy followed by a tailored heat treatment designed to induce in situ precipitation of nano-scale TiC that localizes at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Alloy synthesis via arc melting followed by homogenization; post-synthesis annealing at approximately 900°C for 2 hours in an inert (argon) atmosphere with controlled cooling. Subsequent mechanical tests (e.g., compressive strength) and caloric measurements (under applied magnetic and pressure fields) are performed at room temperature and moderate strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale TiC precipitates formed at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Titanium addition is expected to react with carbon impurities or intentional slight carbon doping to form finely dispersed TiC particles. These nano-precipitates reinforce the grain boundaries, reduce crack initiation and propagation, and thereby enhance the overall mechanical integrity. Their small size and limited volume fraction should not interfere substantially with the intrinsic caloric phase transition in the MM′X material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved compressive strength and fracture toughness (targeting improvements to or above 218 MPa) while maintaining the caloric response—i.e. similar magnitude of caloric effects (magneto- and barocaloric response) to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy which tends to crack under operating conditions despite its large caloric response.
generation.boundary: Operation under the applied-field and pressure-field regimes used in prior studies; mechanical testing at room temperature with standard moderate strain rates; heat treatment parameters fixed around 900°C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative influence on caloric performance is uncertain; over-formation of precipitates or an excessive shift in phase boundaries might slightly alter the caloric transition parameters, so careful optimization of Ti content and heat-treatment conditions is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and one set with 1–3 at% Ti addition. Process both sets under identical melting and annealing conditions (900°C for 2 hours in argon with controlled cooling). Perform mechanical integrity tests (compression tests to measure strength and fracture toughness) and caloric effect measurements (e.g., isothermal entropy change and transition temperature analysis) under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., compressive strength remains below the target or crack propagation is not inhibited) or if the caloric response is reduced by more than approximately 10% relative to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
